log.entry: Commission accepted: PaperAtelier — architecture studio in Old Fenwick

PaperAtelier: Survey what people hate — the review corpus scan — Scanned 31 documented complaint themes in the review corpus. For a architecture studio the primary pains are the 28 universal ones (blocking popups, autoplay, dead links, contact hunts, fluff copy, tracking walls, broken mobile, sameness…) Drawn as secondary risks worth defending against anyway: detail-missing, hidden-prices, shipping-surprise. Total in scope for this build: 31 pains. Every one becomes a demand, every demand becomes rules on the tasks it feeds.
PaperAtelier: Convert the findings into build demands — 31 demands locked. Each is injected as a hard rule into the tasks it feeds (26 task kinds governed).

PaperAtelier: Reason about D1 — OS, input, context — D1 (iOS / Android phones ≤ 640px). Input: touch only — 44px minimum targets, thumb-reach CTA bar. Context: on-the-go, one thumb, interruptions likely. Colour law: high contrast ink on bg; accent reserved for the action bar and key numerals. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D1, never just shrink..

PaperAtelier: Reason about D2 — OS, input, context — D2 (iPadOS / Android tablets 641–1024px). Input: touch + optional keyboard — hover states must be optional. Context: leaning back, longer sessions, comparison reading. Colour law: surface cards on bgAlt bands; accent2 for secondary highlights. D2 gets its own arrangement from the book — the architecture studio reads differently here..

PaperAtelier: Reason about D3 — OS, input, context — D3 (Windows / macOS / ChromeOS laptops 1025–1440px). Input: pointer + keyboard — hover affordances expected. Context: task mode: comparing, shortlisting, filling forms. Colour law: full palette unlocked; ink-panel heroes carry accent numerals. D3 gets its own arrangement from the book — the architecture studio reads differently here..

PaperAtelier: Reason about D4 — OS, input, context — D4 (Windows / macOS desktops 1441–1920px). Input: precise pointer, large canvas — density is welcome. Context: deep work, multi-tab comparison. Colour law: bento/tinted cards in surface + accent washes; mega footer on bgAlt. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D4, never just shrink..

PaperAtelier: Reason about D5 — OS, input, context — D5 (Large displays / TV ≥ 1921px). Input: 10-foot or seated-far viewing — type must scale monumentally. Context: ambient, cinematic, first-impression. Colour law: monumental type on ink or accent2 washes; bgAlt bands alternate. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D5, never just shrink..

PaperAtelier: Reason about colour — what works where — Global colour law locked: hero washes, card tints and CTA styles are chosen per page from RECIPE_POOL — every recipe must clear its WCAG target before it is allowed. The palette (Saffron Quarry, complementary) provides the roles; dark-mode tokens re-derive and re-check.

findings.hate: Pop-ups and interstitials slamming over the page before anything can be read
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — popup/interstitial usability (Nielsen 2004, reconfirmed 2017); Google interstitial penalty (2017)
findings.demand: Nothing blocks the page. Any notice is inline, small and dismissible.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Audio or video that starts playing uninvited
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — most-hated advertising techniques (Nielsen 2004)
findings.demand: Media stays silent until clicked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hero carousels nobody clicks — visitors only ever see slide one
findings.source: Erik Runyon, Carousel Interaction Stats (Notre Dame Web Team, 2013): ~1% engage, 84% see only the first slide
findings.demand: One honest hero; content in static, scannable grids.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pages that take forever — people give up and never come back
findings.source: Google DoubleClick mobile speed study (2016): 53% of mobile visits abandon past 3 seconds
findings.demand: A fast page: light HTML, lazy images, no junk scripts.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Generic stock-photo smiles that scream "nobody actually works here"
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Photos as Web Content (Levin 2011): filler photos erode trust
findings.demand: Real, specific imagery with alt text that says what is actually shown.
findings.bite: a architecture studio sells craft — filler photos would undo the whole story

findings.hate: Being forced to register an account just to look or ask
findings.source: Baymard Institute: roughly one in four abandons when forced to create an account first
findings.demand: Everything works as a guest; accounts optional and honestly labelled.
findings.bite: nobody registers to browse a architecture studio

findings.hate: Digging through pages to find one working phone number
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Contact Us usability: users fail when contact facts are buried
findings.demand: Contact everywhere it is needed: nav, footer, its own page, and a full directory.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: No idea who is behind the site — no names, no address, no history
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — "About Us" usability studies (2006, 2016): users seek the humans
findings.demand: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Squinting at 12px body text
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — 16px+ body-size guidance for aging eyes
findings.demand: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Grey-on-grey text nobody can read
findings.source: WCAG 2.1 contrast minimums (W3C)
findings.demand: Measured contrast, not vibes.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking a link and getting a PDF instead of a page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — PDF: Still Unfit for Web Reading (Nielsen 2001, reconfirmed)
findings.demand: Information as real web pages.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking something and landing on an error
findings.source: Nielsen — the original web usability heuristics: broken links destroy credibility
findings.demand: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Marketing fog — "best-in-class world-class synergy"
findings.source: Morkes & Nielsen, How Users Read on the Web (1997): users scan; fluff is skipped
findings.demand: Plain words, concrete nouns, real numbers.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Fake countdowns, fake scarcity, unsubscribe mazes
findings.source: Brignull — Deceptive Design registry (darkpatterns.org, 2010)
findings.demand: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Another cookie banner to wrestle before reading one sentence
findings.source: EU consent-fatigue reporting + EDPB guidance on deceptive consent flows
findings.demand: No banner because no tracking.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Proving humanity nine times to send one message
findings.source: Recurring public complaint theme around CAPTCHA gates (widely reported UX rage)
findings.demand: A form that just sends.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pinch-zooming a site that pretends phones do not exist
findings.source: Google mobile UX guidance: 44px tap targets, viewport sanity
findings.demand: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A bottomless feed — never finding the thing twice
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Infinite Scrolling Is Not for Every Website (2013)
findings.demand: Finite, findable grids with an end.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: The menu rearranging itself on every page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — navigation consistency heuristics
findings.demand: The same nav, same spot, every page.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A big site with no way to search it
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — site search usability: search is the lifeline on content-heavy sites
findings.demand: A search that actually finds things.
findings.bite: the catalog and journal make this site big enough to need search

findings.hate: Sites that screen readers and keyboards cannot use
findings.source: WHO disability statistics (1.3 billion people); WCAG 2.1
findings.demand: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Forms demanding a life story to ask one question
findings.source: Recurring form-usability finding (NN/g form design usability)
findings.demand: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Every template site looks identical — the hero, the cards, the footer, all the same
findings.source: The recurring public complaint "all websites look the same" (long-running theme in web/UX discourse, e.g. template-sameness threads on Hacker News and The Verge)
findings.demand: A site that was arranged, not assembled from the first template on the shelf.
findings.bite: a architecture studio site that looks like every template loses the trust it needs

findings.hate: Sharing a link and the preview card is broken or empty
findings.source: Open Graph protocol spec (Facebook/Meta) + universal share-card complaints
findings.demand: A real preview image and honest title/description.
findings.bite: the architecture studio spreads by sharing — broken cards kill the share

findings.hate: Galleries of grey placeholder boxes
findings.source: Recurring marketplace/portfolio review complaint: shipped sites with empty media
findings.demand: Every image slot filled with real bytes before the site ships.
findings.bite: visual proof is the architecture studio's best argument

findings.hate: Legal pages written to be unreadable
findings.source: Plain-language movement (e.g. US PLAIN Act principles applied to web policies)
findings.demand: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A 2019 copyright in the footer — instantly reads as abandoned
findings.source: Recurring credibility-review theme: stale dates signal neglect
findings.demand: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Testimonials that read like they were written by the owner at 2am
findings.source: FTC endorsement guides + recurring trust-review complaints about fake-sounding reviews
findings.demand: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Product pages with three words and a photo — no specs, no sizes, no proof
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — e-commerce product page usability: users decide on details, not vibes
findings.demand: A detail page that answers the questions before they are asked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hunting for a price that is nowhere on the site
findings.source: Baymard Institute checkout research (annual): surprise costs are a leading abandonment cause
findings.demand: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
findings.bite: a architecture studio visitor decides on price — hide it and they leave

findings.hate: Getting to the last step and discovering extra fees
findings.source: Baymard Institute: extra costs are the top checkout-abandonment cause (annual study)
findings.demand: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

brief.promise: Buildings that hold light. PaperAtelier keeps that promise in Old Fenwick.
brief.cityStory: The studio works at the seam between landscape and structure — and we do it in Old Fenwick.

D1.why: Quiet Grid — Small uniform cards run 2-up at 12px gaps — built for comparing many items on one screen. (source: Dense 2-col phone grid (Material image lists))

D2.why: Ribbon CTA — A slim accent CTA band runs between every two sections — the ribbon is the rhythm. (source: Interspersed CTA bands (conversion pattern))

D3.why: Monolith Body — Full-bleed dark hero; body sections run a strict 720px measure on paper. (source: v2 Monolith family at laptop)

D4.why: Showcase 4:4 — Perfect 4/4 split: copy left, framed artifact right; proof row of 4 beneath. (source: Equal split with framed artifact (gallery convention))

D5.why: Panoramic — A 21/9 media band is the hero; content runs a 1560 container beneath. (source: Ultrawide media band (video convention))

rules: One thought per element — never blend two ideas into one block.

log.entry: Commission accepted: River & Little — yoga atelier in Ashford

River & Little: Survey what people hate — the review corpus scan — Scanned 31 documented complaint themes in the review corpus. For a yoga atelier the primary pains are the 28 universal ones (blocking popups, autoplay, dead links, contact hunts, fluff copy, tracking walls, broken mobile, sameness…) plus the commerce pains that bite this niche hardest: hidden-prices, shipping-surprise, detail-missing. Total in scope for this build: 31 pains. Every one becomes a demand, every demand becomes rules on the tasks it feeds.
River & Little: Convert the findings into build demands — 31 demands locked. Each is injected as a hard rule into the tasks it feeds (26 task kinds governed).

findings.hate: Pop-ups and interstitials slamming over the page before anything can be read
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — popup/interstitial usability (Nielsen 2004, reconfirmed 2017); Google interstitial penalty (2017)
findings.demand: Nothing blocks the page. Any notice is inline, small and dismissible.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Audio or video that starts playing uninvited
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — most-hated advertising techniques (Nielsen 2004)
findings.demand: Media stays silent until clicked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hero carousels nobody clicks — visitors only ever see slide one
findings.source: Erik Runyon, Carousel Interaction Stats (Notre Dame Web Team, 2013): ~1% engage, 84% see only the first slide
findings.demand: One honest hero; content in static, scannable grids.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pages that take forever — people give up and never come back
findings.source: Google DoubleClick mobile speed study (2016): 53% of mobile visits abandon past 3 seconds
findings.demand: A fast page: light HTML, lazy images, no junk scripts.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Generic stock-photo smiles that scream "nobody actually works here"
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Photos as Web Content (Levin 2011): filler photos erode trust
findings.demand: Real, specific imagery with alt text that says what is actually shown.
findings.bite: a yoga atelier sells craft — filler photos would undo the whole story

findings.hate: Being forced to register an account just to look or ask
findings.source: Baymard Institute: roughly one in four abandons when forced to create an account first
findings.demand: Everything works as a guest; accounts optional and honestly labelled.
findings.bite: nobody registers to browse a yoga atelier

findings.hate: Digging through pages to find one working phone number
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Contact Us usability: users fail when contact facts are buried
findings.demand: Contact everywhere it is needed: nav, footer, its own page, and a full directory.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: No idea who is behind the site — no names, no address, no history
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — "About Us" usability studies (2006, 2016): users seek the humans
findings.demand: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Squinting at 12px body text
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — 16px+ body-size guidance for aging eyes
findings.demand: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Grey-on-grey text nobody can read
findings.source: WCAG 2.1 contrast minimums (W3C)
findings.demand: Measured contrast, not vibes.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking a link and getting a PDF instead of a page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — PDF: Still Unfit for Web Reading (Nielsen 2001, reconfirmed)
findings.demand: Information as real web pages.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking something and landing on an error
findings.source: Nielsen — the original web usability heuristics: broken links destroy credibility
findings.demand: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Marketing fog — "best-in-class world-class synergy"
findings.source: Morkes & Nielsen, How Users Read on the Web (1997): users scan; fluff is skipped
findings.demand: Plain words, concrete nouns, real numbers.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Fake countdowns, fake scarcity, unsubscribe mazes
findings.source: Brignull — Deceptive Design registry (darkpatterns.org, 2010)
findings.demand: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Another cookie banner to wrestle before reading one sentence
findings.source: EU consent-fatigue reporting + EDPB guidance on deceptive consent flows
findings.demand: No banner because no tracking.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Proving humanity nine times to send one message
findings.source: Recurring public complaint theme around CAPTCHA gates (widely reported UX rage)
findings.demand: A form that just sends.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pinch-zooming a site that pretends phones do not exist
findings.source: Google mobile UX guidance: 44px tap targets, viewport sanity
findings.demand: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A bottomless feed — never finding the thing twice
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Infinite Scrolling Is Not for Every Website (2013)
findings.demand: Finite, findable grids with an end.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: The menu rearranging itself on every page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — navigation consistency heuristics
findings.demand: The same nav, same spot, every page.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A big site with no way to search it
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — site search usability: search is the lifeline on content-heavy sites
findings.demand: A search that actually finds things.
findings.bite: the catalog and journal make this site big enough to need search

findings.hate: Sites that screen readers and keyboards cannot use
findings.source: WHO disability statistics (1.3 billion people); WCAG 2.1
findings.demand: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Forms demanding a life story to ask one question
findings.source: Recurring form-usability finding (NN/g form design usability)
findings.demand: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Every template site looks identical — the hero, the cards, the footer, all the same
findings.source: The recurring public complaint "all websites look the same" (long-running theme in web/UX discourse, e.g. template-sameness threads on Hacker News and The Verge)
findings.demand: A site that was arranged, not assembled from the first template on the shelf.
findings.bite: a yoga atelier site that looks like every template loses the trust it needs

findings.hate: Sharing a link and the preview card is broken or empty
findings.source: Open Graph protocol spec (Facebook/Meta) + universal share-card complaints
findings.demand: A real preview image and honest title/description.
findings.bite: the yoga atelier spreads by sharing — broken cards kill the share

findings.hate: Galleries of grey placeholder boxes
findings.source: Recurring marketplace/portfolio review complaint: shipped sites with empty media
findings.demand: Every image slot filled with real bytes before the site ships.
findings.bite: visual proof is the yoga atelier's best argument

findings.hate: Legal pages written to be unreadable
findings.source: Plain-language movement (e.g. US PLAIN Act principles applied to web policies)
findings.demand: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A 2019 copyright in the footer — instantly reads as abandoned
findings.source: Recurring credibility-review theme: stale dates signal neglect
findings.demand: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Testimonials that read like they were written by the owner at 2am
findings.source: FTC endorsement guides + recurring trust-review complaints about fake-sounding reviews
findings.demand: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hunting for a price that is nowhere on the site
findings.source: Baymard Institute checkout research (annual): surprise costs are a leading abandonment cause
findings.demand: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
findings.bite: a yoga atelier visitor decides on price — hide it and they leave

findings.hate: Getting to the last step and discovering extra fees
findings.source: Baymard Institute: extra costs are the top checkout-abandonment cause (annual study)
findings.demand: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Product pages with three words and a photo — no specs, no sizes, no proof
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — e-commerce product page usability: users decide on details, not vibes
findings.demand: A detail page that answers the questions before they are asked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

log.entry: Commission accepted: The Amber Swell — surf school in Kirkwall

The Amber Swell: Survey what people hate — the review corpus scan — Scanned 31 documented complaint themes in the review corpus. For a surf school the primary pains are the 28 universal ones (blocking popups, autoplay, dead links, contact hunts, fluff copy, tracking walls, broken mobile, sameness…) plus the commerce pains that bite this niche hardest: hidden-prices, shipping-surprise, detail-missing. Total in scope for this build: 31 pains. Every one becomes a demand, every demand becomes rules on the tasks it feeds.
The Amber Swell: Convert the findings into build demands — 31 demands locked. Each is injected as a hard rule into the tasks it feeds (26 task kinds governed).
The Amber Swell: Compose visitor persona 1 of 3 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — persona 1 of 3
The Amber Swell: Compose visitor persona 2 of 3 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — persona 2 of 3
The Amber Swell: Compose visitor persona 3 of 3 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — persona 3 of 3
The Amber Swell: Map the journey of persona 1 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — journey 1 of 3
The Amber Swell: Map the journey of persona 2 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — journey 2 of 3
The Amber Swell: Map the journey of persona 3 — 3 personas composed from the findings; each journey's friction points map to locked demands. — journey 3 of 3

The Amber Swell: Reason about D1 — OS, input, context — D1 (iOS / Android phones ≤ 640px). Input: touch only — 44px minimum targets, thumb-reach CTA bar. Context: on-the-go, one thumb, interruptions likely. Colour law: high contrast ink on bg; accent reserved for the action bar and key numerals. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D1, never just shrink..

The Amber Swell: Reason about D2 — OS, input, context — D2 (iPadOS / Android tablets 641–1024px). Input: touch + optional keyboard — hover states must be optional. Context: leaning back, longer sessions, comparison reading. Colour law: surface cards on bgAlt bands; accent2 for secondary highlights. D2 gets its own arrangement from the book — the surf school reads differently here..

The Amber Swell: Reason about D3 — OS, input, context — D3 (Windows / macOS / ChromeOS laptops 1025–1440px). Input: pointer + keyboard — hover affordances expected. Context: task mode: comparing, shortlisting, filling forms. Colour law: full palette unlocked; ink-panel heroes carry accent numerals. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D3, never just shrink..

The Amber Swell: Reason about D4 — OS, input, context — D4 (Windows / macOS desktops 1441–1920px). Input: precise pointer, large canvas — density is welcome. Context: deep work, multi-tab comparison. Colour law: bento/tinted cards in surface + accent washes; mega footer on bgAlt. D4 gets its own arrangement from the book — the surf school reads differently here..

The Amber Swell: Reason about D5 — OS, input, context — D5 (Large displays / TV ≥ 1921px). Input: 10-foot or seated-far viewing — type must scale monumentally. Context: ambient, cinematic, first-impression. Colour law: monumental type on ink or accent2 washes; bgAlt bands alternate. D5 gets its own arrangement from the book — the surf school reads differently here..

The Amber Swell: Reason about colour — what works where — Global colour law locked: hero washes, card tints and CTA styles are chosen per page from RECIPE_POOL — every recipe must clear its WCAG target before it is allowed. The palette (Iris Tide, complementary) provides the roles; dark-mode tokens re-derive and re-check.
The Amber Swell: Lock the brief — audience, tone, promise — deterministic solver — brief composed from niche grammar, consistent with the reasoner’s findings
The Amber Swell: Lock the palette — harmony math + WCAG — deterministic solver — harmony math + WCAG battery already passed
The Amber Swell: Choose the D1 archetype — deterministic solver — brief-fit archetype from 20 D1 layouts
The Amber Swell: Choose the D2 archetype — deterministic solver — brief-fit archetype from 23 D2 layouts
The Amber Swell: Choose the D3 archetype — deterministic solver — brief-fit archetype from 25 D3 layouts
The Amber Swell: Choose the D4 archetype — deterministic solver — brief-fit archetype from 24 D4 layouts
The Amber Swell: Choose the D5 archetype — deterministic solver — brief-fit archetype from 20 D5 layouts

The Amber Swell: Reason about the catalog — what the products must do — Catalog law for 0 products: prices visible at the listing level — the surf school visitor should never click to learn a price. Each product earns its own detail page, its own image slot, its own alt text.
The Amber Swell: Plan the page map — every page earns its slot — deterministic solver — 16 pages planned (content + functional, multi-page mandate)

findings.hate: Pop-ups and interstitials slamming over the page before anything can be read
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — popup/interstitial usability (Nielsen 2004, reconfirmed 2017); Google interstitial penalty (2017)
findings.demand: Nothing blocks the page. Any notice is inline, small and dismissible.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Audio or video that starts playing uninvited
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — most-hated advertising techniques (Nielsen 2004)
findings.demand: Media stays silent until clicked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hero carousels nobody clicks — visitors only ever see slide one
findings.source: Erik Runyon, Carousel Interaction Stats (Notre Dame Web Team, 2013): ~1% engage, 84% see only the first slide
findings.demand: One honest hero; content in static, scannable grids.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pages that take forever — people give up and never come back
findings.source: Google DoubleClick mobile speed study (2016): 53% of mobile visits abandon past 3 seconds
findings.demand: A fast page: light HTML, lazy images, no junk scripts.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Generic stock-photo smiles that scream "nobody actually works here"
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Photos as Web Content (Levin 2011): filler photos erode trust
findings.demand: Real, specific imagery with alt text that says what is actually shown.
findings.bite: a surf school sells craft — filler photos would undo the whole story

findings.hate: Being forced to register an account just to look or ask
findings.source: Baymard Institute: roughly one in four abandons when forced to create an account first
findings.demand: Everything works as a guest; accounts optional and honestly labelled.
findings.bite: nobody registers to browse a surf school

findings.hate: Digging through pages to find one working phone number
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Contact Us usability: users fail when contact facts are buried
findings.demand: Contact everywhere it is needed: nav, footer, its own page, and a full directory.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: No idea who is behind the site — no names, no address, no history
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — "About Us" usability studies (2006, 2016): users seek the humans
findings.demand: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Squinting at 12px body text
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — 16px+ body-size guidance for aging eyes
findings.demand: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Grey-on-grey text nobody can read
findings.source: WCAG 2.1 contrast minimums (W3C)
findings.demand: Measured contrast, not vibes.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking a link and getting a PDF instead of a page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — PDF: Still Unfit for Web Reading (Nielsen 2001, reconfirmed)
findings.demand: Information as real web pages.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking something and landing on an error
findings.source: Nielsen — the original web usability heuristics: broken links destroy credibility
findings.demand: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Marketing fog — "best-in-class world-class synergy"
findings.source: Morkes & Nielsen, How Users Read on the Web (1997): users scan; fluff is skipped
findings.demand: Plain words, concrete nouns, real numbers.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Fake countdowns, fake scarcity, unsubscribe mazes
findings.source: Brignull — Deceptive Design registry (darkpatterns.org, 2010)
findings.demand: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Another cookie banner to wrestle before reading one sentence
findings.source: EU consent-fatigue reporting + EDPB guidance on deceptive consent flows
findings.demand: No banner because no tracking.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Proving humanity nine times to send one message
findings.source: Recurring public complaint theme around CAPTCHA gates (widely reported UX rage)
findings.demand: A form that just sends.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pinch-zooming a site that pretends phones do not exist
findings.source: Google mobile UX guidance: 44px tap targets, viewport sanity
findings.demand: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A bottomless feed — never finding the thing twice
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Infinite Scrolling Is Not for Every Website (2013)
findings.demand: Finite, findable grids with an end.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: The menu rearranging itself on every page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — navigation consistency heuristics
findings.demand: The same nav, same spot, every page.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A big site with no way to search it
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — site search usability: search is the lifeline on content-heavy sites
findings.demand: A search that actually finds things.
findings.bite: the catalog and journal make this site big enough to need search

findings.hate: Sites that screen readers and keyboards cannot use
findings.source: WHO disability statistics (1.3 billion people); WCAG 2.1
findings.demand: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Forms demanding a life story to ask one question
findings.source: Recurring form-usability finding (NN/g form design usability)
findings.demand: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Every template site looks identical — the hero, the cards, the footer, all the same
findings.source: The recurring public complaint "all websites look the same" (long-running theme in web/UX discourse, e.g. template-sameness threads on Hacker News and The Verge)
findings.demand: A site that was arranged, not assembled from the first template on the shelf.
findings.bite: a surf school site that looks like every template loses the trust it needs

findings.hate: Sharing a link and the preview card is broken or empty
findings.source: Open Graph protocol spec (Facebook/Meta) + universal share-card complaints
findings.demand: A real preview image and honest title/description.
findings.bite: the surf school spreads by sharing — broken cards kill the share

findings.hate: Galleries of grey placeholder boxes
findings.source: Recurring marketplace/portfolio review complaint: shipped sites with empty media
findings.demand: Every image slot filled with real bytes before the site ships.
findings.bite: visual proof is the surf school's best argument

findings.hate: Legal pages written to be unreadable
findings.source: Plain-language movement (e.g. US PLAIN Act principles applied to web policies)
findings.demand: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A 2019 copyright in the footer — instantly reads as abandoned
findings.source: Recurring credibility-review theme: stale dates signal neglect
findings.demand: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Testimonials that read like they were written by the owner at 2am
findings.source: FTC endorsement guides + recurring trust-review complaints about fake-sounding reviews
findings.demand: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hunting for a price that is nowhere on the site
findings.source: Baymard Institute checkout research (annual): surprise costs are a leading abandonment cause
findings.demand: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
findings.bite: a surf school visitor decides on price — hide it and they leave

findings.hate: Getting to the last step and discovering extra fees
findings.source: Baymard Institute: extra costs are the top checkout-abandonment cause (annual study)
findings.demand: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Product pages with three words and a photo — no specs, no sizes, no proof
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — e-commerce product page usability: users decide on details, not vibes
findings.demand: A detail page that answers the questions before they are asked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

D2.colours: hero is an #201e29 panel with #f7f6f8 type — the accent pops numerals; cards sit on #ffffff with  hairlines; CTAs are solid #819617 with #819617 text. On D2, surface cards on bgAlt bands; accent2 for secondary highlights.
D2.productsNeeded: needs the 6 services as cards
D2.deviceOs: iPadOS / Android tablets 641–1024px — touch + optional keyboard — hover states must be optional. Context: leaning back, longer sessions, comparison reading.

D3.name: Aurora — Centered Statement
D3.why: Aurora: Single center axis. Kicker → H1 → lede → two CTAs stacked down the middle; stats band dark; cards 3-up. Reading: Z. Source: Z-pattern for low-density pages (NN/g); Material 12-col responsive grid.
D3.colours: hero is an #201e29 panel with #f7f6f8 type — the accent pops numerals; cards sit on #ffffff with  hairlines; CTAs are solid #819617 with #819617 text. On D3, full palette unlocked; ink-panel heroes carry accent numerals.
D3.deviceOs: Windows / macOS / ChromeOS laptops 1025–1440px — pointer + keyboard — hover affordances expected. Context: task mode: comparing, shortlisting, filling forms.

D4.name: Atlas Mega — Sidebar + 4 Cols
D4.why: Atlas Mega: Sidebar persists; content runs 4-col rows with alternating skeletons. Reading: Spotted. Source: v2 Atlas at desktop width.
D4.colours: hero is an #201e29 panel with #f7f6f8 type — the accent pops numerals; cards sit on #ffffff with  hairlines; CTAs are solid #819617 with #819617 text. On D4, bento/tinted cards in surface + accent washes; mega footer on bgAlt.
D4.deviceOs: Windows / macOS desktops 1441–1920px — precise pointer, large canvas — density is welcome. Context: deep work, multi-tab comparison.

D5.name: Skyline — Silhouette Stats
D5.why: Skyline: Stat towers render as a filled skyline silhouette against the ambient field. Reading: Layer-cake. Source: Stat towers as a silhouette band.
D5.colours: hero is an #201e29 panel with #f7f6f8 type — the accent pops numerals; cards sit on #ffffff with  hairlines; CTAs are solid #819617 with #819617 text. On D5, monumental type on ink or accent2 washes; bgAlt bands alternate.
D5.deviceOs: Large displays / TV ≥ 1921px — 10-foot or seated-far viewing — type must scale monumentally. Context: ambient, cinematic, first-impression.
